thread.title: Code name Kale: How the data center world is keeping its Loudoun projects a secret

author: Michael Neibauer
title: Code name Kale: How the data center world is keeping its Loudoun projects a secret
text: – Associate Editor, Washington Business Journal Apr 18, 2018, 11:46am EDT Updated Apr 18, 2018, 1:35pm EDT What is the common thread between a data center and kale? Seriously, I have no idea. And that's apparently the point. In Loudoun County, a global hub for data centers, an increasing number of developers or their consultants are code-naming their projects to keep them a secret — either from the public or the county itself. These projects are usually exempt from Freedom of Information Act requests and often involve the biggest names in tech, from Google (NASDAQ: GOOG) to Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) to Amazon Web Services (NASDAQ: AMZN). The latest is “Project Kale,” described in fresh Loudoun planning documents as a 288,000-square-foot data center slated for a site on the north side of the Dulles Greenway, southwest of Luck Stone Quarry. The applicant is listed as Hayden Technologies LLC, a Charlotte, North Carolina-based consultant. The end user is not listed. And the connection to kale, the antioxidant-soaked leafy green vegetable, is not explained. Buddy Rizer , director of Loudoun’s Department of Economic Development, said code-naming is a pretty standard practice, though the volume of odd names is on the rise as the number of data center projects soar. Other code names Loudoun has used in the past: Motion , Viper, Buffalo, Libra, Independence, Seam head, Seal and Legacy. This secretive strategy is popular elsewhere, too. In Henrico County, Facebook (NASDAQ: FB) called its $1 billion data center "Project Echo" for a time . In Oregon, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) used the code name "Maverick." Loudoun has 10 million square feet of operating data center space, with 4.5 million more square feet under construction — and new proposals are submitted to the county's pipeline seemingly every day. Virtually every player in the data center market has a stake in the Northern Virginia jurisdiction. “A lot of projects we work with are confidential at the client's request, sometimes for contractual, security or competitive reasons,” Rizer said in an email. “To assist in the confidentiality, we often refer to these projects by a code name until a public announcement is made. Sometimes a consultant or project team will bring us the project without disclosing the end user, sometimes the company will name it, sometimes we name it. We usually try to have a little fun with it.” And in doing so, drive this reporter crazy. – Associate Editor, Washington Business Journal Apr 18, 2018, 11:46am EDT Updated Apr 18, 2018, 1:35pm EDT Related Content
